column4: The source section names the root م ن ن and its dictionary sense of fatigue that cuts a traveler off from the road. This verse records thirst, fatigue, hunger, and each campaign step as good deeds, then says God does not let good-doers' reward be lost.

The source section's dictionary form اليعملة names a she-camel made for work and الرد names camel backs and loads. Here spending and crossing a valley are each recorded as deeds, making the animal-road image a measure of human effort that is not wasted.

The source section's dictionary form بَلِيد describes a horse falling behind and a person weakening even in generosity. This verse joins giving wealth with patience in hardship and battle, portraying the sustained generosity and endurance that answer that decline.

The section's weary road, work, battle charge, and uncut wage meet in this account of migration, expulsion, harm, fighting, and being slain: God promises to erase their wrongs and admit them to gardens, explicitly saying no worker's deed is lost.

The source section sets labor and travel against fatigue and asks who keeps going. This verse says a person has only what he strives for, turning the image of sustained work into personal responsibility.

As the next step after 53:39, this verse says that striving will be seen. It supplies the reckoning of the labor that the source section links to a lasting wage; its own contribution is that effort is brought into view.
Following 53:39–40, this verse says the striving will be repaid in full. That is the closest counterpart here to the source section's reward that is not cut off after a tiring road.

The source section explicitly invokes this verse: a person is striving toward the Lord and will meet Him. It gives the tired mount's road a human and final destination, in the verse's own account of labor.

The source section explicitly invokes the claim that humanity was created in hardship. It makes the tiring road more than an animal scene: human life itself is arduous, against which the section sets an uncut reward.

The source section's dictionary form الرد names camel backs and load-bearing camels; this verse says livestock carry people's heavy loads to distant places they could not reach without great hardship. It directly stages the burdened journey and the human strain beside it.

The source section develops dependable and exhausted camels on a journey. This verse depicts pilgrims arriving on lean camels from distant passes, a direct image of animals and people enduring a long route toward a destination.

The source section describes a lagging horse and a warrior whose charge may fail to last. This oath opens with steeds running while panting, a specific counter-image of mounts that continue their charge under strain.

Continuing the charge begun in 100:1, this verse adds sparks struck by the horses' hooves. Its own contribution is the force and speed of the sustained advance described in the source section's warrior image.
As the next beat of the same horse-charge sequence, this verse has the steeds raid at dawn. It gives the source section's possible attack a concrete continuation beyond the initial rush.

This neighbor to 100:1–3 adds dust raised by the rushing horses. It makes the charge's ongoing movement visible, answering the section's image of an assault that might falter before it is carried through.

The sequence ends with the horses plunging into the midst of the gathering. This supplies the completed attack that contrasts with the source section's dictionary example of a warrior who attacks and then fails to prove true in the charge.

The section's warrior may weaken after attacking; this verse describes fighters who did not lose heart, weaken, or give in after suffering in battle. It is a direct contrary example of endurance under attack.

The source section's dictionary form الأليس describes a warrior who does not leave his opponent, while its kadhaba example is a charge not sustained. This verse commands believers not to turn their backs when they meet an advancing enemy.

This neighbor completes 8:15's command by naming the exceptions for a tactical maneuver or joining another unit; otherwise retreat draws God's anger. It marks the boundary between a feint and the faltering charge in the source section.
The section asks who endures and who is spent in the warriors' world. This verse commands fighters who meet a force to stand firm and remember God, a direct account of maintaining resolve in battle.

Continuing 8:45's battle guidance, this verse warns that disputing will make the fighters fail and lose strength, then commands patience. Its own contribution names the collapse of resolve that the section's exhausted mount and failed charge evoke.

The source section's dictionary explanation of كذب says a warrior attacked but did not prove true in the charge. This verse describes men true to their covenant with God, some of whom fulfilled their pledge without changing; it is the precise opposite of breaking under pressure.

The source section's dictionary account of كذب (in the warrior branch) describes an attack not carried through. This verse contrasts breaking a pledge with fulfilling it and promises a great reward for fulfillment, a moral counterpart to the charge that holds and the wage that continues.

The source section explicitly reads غير ممنون as reward not cut off and gives the root م ن ن's fatigue and weak-rope senses. This verse repeats the exact phrase for the reward of believers who do good, linking the lexical image to its stated recompense.

The source section explicitly glosses غير ممنون as an uncut reward. This verse uses the same phrase for believers who do good, so its own claim directly sustains the image's promise of wages beyond exhaustion.

The source section links a tiring road to reward that does not cease. This verse describes someone who leaves home migrating toward God and His Messenger, then is overtaken by death before arrival; the verse still guarantees the reward, showing that the road's interruption does not end it.

The source section opposes a mount and traveler giving out to a reward that remains. This verse contrasts what is with people and perishes with what is with God and endures, then promises patient people their reward for their deeds.

The source section turns on who can endure and who is exhausted before receiving recompense. This verse promises patient people their reward without measure, connecting endurance to a wage that is not diminished by the road.
The source section says the road's final reward is uncut. This verse says the reward of anyone who does good works will not be lost, making the labor-to-wage relation explicit.

The source section contrasts tiring effort with enduring recompense. This verse commands patience and says God does not waste the reward of those who do good, a direct assurance that effort held through hardship counts.
After 84:6's person striving toward the Lord, this verse introduces the one given his record in his right hand. It supplies the favorable reckoning that follows the labor named in the cited verse.
Continuing 84:6–7, this verse says the person with the record in the right hand will be given an easy reckoning. Its own contribution is a favorable accounting after the section's long road of work.
This neighbor completes the favorable outcome of 84:7–8: the person returns to his people rejoicing. It makes the successful end of the toil a return rather than exhaustion.

The source section's dictionary form الرد is explained as camel backs and load-bearing camels. This verse explicitly distinguishes load-bearing livestock from animals close to the ground, giving a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the section's animal-load vocabulary.

The source section's dictionary form الرد names the backs of load-bearing camels. This verse says people settle on animals' backs and remember their Lord when they are mounted, making the rider's dependence on the back that carries him explicit.

The section's dictionary form الرد names load-bearing camel backs, and its al-amūn is a trusted travel mount. This verse says people are carried on livestock and ships and reach needs they hold in their hearts, showing the route and destination those mounts serve.

The source section labels the root ء م ن and connects it to the dependable she-camel, trusted not to tire or stumble. This verse describes believers who keep their trusts and covenants, giving human conduct the same specific quality of reliability.

The source section's dictionary form الأمون names a camel trusted not to falter. This verse repeats the description of those who keep their trusts and covenants, applying that reliability to people and their commitments.

The source section labels the root ء م ن through a mount trusted not to fail its traveler. This verse treats a human trustee as responsible for returning what was entrusted to them, a specific moral counterpart to being trusted with a load.
The source section's al-amūn is a mount trusted to carry a traveler safely. This verse commands that entrusted trusts be returned to their owners, carrying the same reliability into human dealings.

The source section stages animals traveling on a road. This neighboring verse describes livestock being driven out and brought back in the evening; its own contribution is the daily movement of the mounts before 16:7's long haul of heavy loads.

This neighbor to 16:7 names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding. It broadens the load-bearing livestock in the previous verse to the riding and war-horse world that the source section develops.

This verse introduces the livestock that people ride and eat, immediately before 40:80 says they are carried on them toward their needs. It gives the source section's riding animals their created purpose in that passage.

This verse introduces ships and livestock as things people ride, before 43:13 names settling on their backs and remembering God. It supplies the travel-mount setting for the source section's camel-back dictionary sense.

The source section repeatedly develops the camel as a trustworthy or burden-bearing mount. This verse directly directs attention to camels and how they were created, inviting the reader to consider the animal whose endurance the section's dictionary forms evoke.
The source section places its image in the world of warriors and horses. This verse names tethered horses as part of preparing for battle, giving the riding animal a concrete martial role.

The source section explicitly invokes human hardship and develops the tiring road. This verse names the steep ascent that a person has failed to undertake, giving the difficult path a concrete moral form.

This neighbor explains the steep ascent named in 90:11 and frames the actions described in 90:13–17. It makes the source section's arduous path a concrete moral ascent, not a vague metaphor for hardship.
As the first description of 90:11–12's steep ascent, this verse names freeing a person from bondage. It makes costly action part of the road that the source section associates with endurance.
Continuing the ascent's description, this verse names feeding during a day of hunger. It directly joins the source section's road hardship to its dictionary sense of weakness even in generosity.

This neighbor specifies one recipient of the feeding in 90:14: an orphan who is a relative. It makes the ascent's generosity concrete, matching the source section's emphasis on not weakening in giving.

This neighbor adds the needy person in severe poverty as another recipient on the ascent. Its own contribution is the concrete object of generosity that the source section contrasts with weakening even in giving.

This verse completes the steep-ascent passage with mutual exhortation to patience and compassion. It joins endurance to care for others, the quality needed not to give out on the road or in generosity.

The source section's dictionary explanation of بَلَد describes becoming weak even in generosity. This verse describes people who give in both ease and hardship and pardon others, the specific opposite of failing in generosity when conditions are hard.

The source section explicitly gives the dictionary form المنين as a weak rope. This verse commands people to hold fast to God's rope together, a precise image of a bond meant to sustain rather than give way.

The source section's dictionary account of كذب describes an attack that begins but is not carried through. This verse asks why believers say what they do not do, making failure to enact one's word a concrete counterpart to that unfinished charge.

This neighbor states that it is deeply hateful to God to say what one does not do. It supplies the judgment on the word-action gap that 61:2 raises, matching the source section's account of an assault that fails to prove true.

After 61:2–3's warning against words without action, this verse describes fighters who stand in ranks like a solid structure. Its own contribution is a picture of battle action held together, opposite to the warrior who falters mid-charge.
This verse completes 53:39–41's sequence of striving, being seen, and being repaid: the ultimate destination is the Lord. It gives the source section's arduous road a stated endpoint.

The source section's human moves from best formation to a lowered state, alongside the image of a mount that tires and stops. This verse says some people are returned to the feeblest age, a specific bodily decline after life and strength.

The source section turns from humanity's best formation to being brought low. This verse describes some people being returned to the feeblest age, when knowledge fades, giving that descent a concrete human course.

The source section's image turns from strength and formation toward weakness and exhaustion. This verse explicitly describes creation in weakness, strength after weakness, and weakness again in old age, a direct human reversal of bodily endurance.

As the contrary outcome to 84:7–9, this verse describes the person receiving his record from behind his back. It supplies a failed reckoning beside the source section's contrast between those who endure and those who fall short.
Continuing the contrary outcome begun in 84:10, this verse says the person will call for destruction. Its own contribution is the despair that follows the failed account.
This final neighbor to 84:10–11 names the blazing fire the person enters. It completes the passage's adverse destination, a boundary to the source section's uncut reward.

The source section's dictionary form الأمون is a she-camel trusted not to tire or stumble. This verse warns believers not to betray God, the Messenger, or their trusts, marking the moral opposite of that dependable carrier.

The source section's dictionary form الأليس names a camel carrying every load. This verse sets a specific boundary: no bearer carries another's burden. The next verses 53:39–41 add each person's own striving and recompense; this verse's contribution is the limit on transferring a load.

The source section's dictionary form بليد is a horse that comes behind the leading horses, and the related verb describes falling back in work. This verse tells people to race one another in good deeds, turning the lagging-race image toward action.

The source section's dictionary form بليد describes a horse trailing the leaders. This verse tells people to race toward forgiveness and a garden, making lagging behind a moral image of missing the goal.

The source section says the root ب ل د can describe weakening even in generosity. This verse begins a contrast with the person who gives and is mindful of God, making generosity a chosen response rather than the weakness named by the dictionary entry.

Continuing the giving person's description in 92:5, this verse adds belief in the best outcome. It supplies the conviction behind the good work and lasting reward that the source section places at the end of the road.
This neighbor gives the outcome of 92:5–6: God eases that person's way toward ease. It answers the source section's weary-road image with a stated easing of the path for the generous.
This verse begins the contrary case to 92:5 by describing one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient. It directly recalls the source section's image of weakening even in generosity.
Continuing 92:8's withholding, this verse adds denial of the best outcome. It connects the source section's failed endurance and denial to the choice that turns away from generous work.
This verse gives the outcome of 92:8–9: the person's way is eased toward hardship. Its own contribution is a path of increasing difficulty, a specific reversal of 92:7's easing for the giver.

The source section's dictionary form الأليس names a camel able to carry every load, while 7:40 uses a camel at the needle's eye as an impossible passage into the Garden. The link is a specific limit on the load-bearing camel image, though the verse itself concerns those who reject God's signs.

The source section's dictionary form الأليس describes a camel carrying every load and a person able to bear a great load. This verse sets a boundary: God does not charge a soul beyond its capacity, so human moral burden is measured rather than unlimited.
The source section sets the tiring road against an enduring reward. This verse pairs hardship with ease, a specific assurance that exhaustion is not the road's only outcome.
Repeating the hardship-and-ease pairing from 94:5, this verse makes the reassurance deliberate and sustained, matching the source section's contrast between fatigue and reward that does not stop.

The source section's human is described as laboring along a demanding road. This verse tells the addressee to exert himself after finishing one task, expressing continued effort rather than stopping after an initial charge.
This neighbor directs the exertion of 94:7 toward the Lord. It gives continued work the same orientation as 84:6, which the source section explicitly invokes as striving toward one's Lord.

After 33:23's men who stayed true to their covenant, this verse distinguishes the reward of the truthful from punishment of hypocrites. It connects sustained action in the warrior context to the source section's contrast between an enduring wage and failed resolve.

The source section describes a human return from best formation to a low state. This verse says that long life is followed by reversal in creation; it is a close bodily parallel, though it does not specify a journey or mount.

The source section's dictionary explanation of تقوم includes a mount standing still when exhausted. This verse pictures sacrificial camels standing before they fall on their sides; the bodily scene is close, though their stillness here is ritual, not fatigue.

The source section's central image is a tiring mount and traveler on a road. This verse says people will pass through successive stages; reading its riding word as an echo of the mount is uncertain, while its staged human passage is explicit.
